processes.description: A budget coordinator opens the next year's budget round by announcing the due date for the first draft and sending managers a budget questionnaire to fill in and return by a deadline, including a list of their staff positions. Managers reply with their staffing (a one-person region offers its salary if needed) and with revised forecasts, sometimes reworked after checking headcount with HR. Separately, final monthly budget numbers and regional budget versus actual comparison reports are sent out to managers.
steps: The budget coordinator announces the due date for the first draft of next year's budget.
She sends managers a budget questionnaire to fill in and return by a deadline.
Managers list their staff positions, and salaries where asked.
Managers revise their budget forecasts, checking headcount with HR, and send a revised forecast.
Final budget numbers are forwarded once settled.
Budget versus actual comparison reports for a region are distributed to managers.

stalls.summary: A submitted budget is reworked after a session with HR and a revised forecast follows the next day, so the draft goes round twice.
The coordinator sets firm return deadlines for drafts and questionnaires, one written in capitals, which points to inputs coming back late.

automation.approach: A standard budget questionnaire layout prefilled with each manager's current staff positions from HR and last year's figures, with the due date stated once, so managers only confirm or change lines. Budget versus actual comparison reports generated from the ledger on a fixed monthly schedule and sent to the same distribution list.
automation.rationale: The repetitive part is collecting the same staffing and expense lines from each manager and producing the same comparison report each month. A prefilled form cuts the questionnaire work and the rework after HR checks, and a generated report removes manual assembly. Headcount and forecast judgments stay with managers.

work_estimate.rationale: Minutes go to listing staff positions and salaries for the questionnaire, revising a forecast after checking headcount with HR, and preparing a monthly budget versus actual comparison report. A one-person region's staff list takes about 20 minutes; a forecast revision with HR input can reach about 180; mid 60. Pulling actuals and laying out the report are repetitive; staffing and forecast choices are not.

processes.description: External auditors (Arthur Andersen) test the gas trading books monthly and send requests for deal tickets, P&L top sheets as of a month end, MTM valuation mini-books, the index used to price a deal, and descriptions of where a deal's value comes from. One desk coordinator receives these, forwards them to the traders, schedulers or risk staff who hold the data, collects their answers and passes them back to the auditors, and tracks the requests in a quarterly matrix. Requests for the West desk are routed to other staff.
steps: Auditors send a testing request for deal tickets, a P&L top sheet, valuations or deal support.
The desk coordinator forwards the request to the staff who hold the data, sending West desk items to Pat Ryder.
Staff pull the deal tickets, confirmations, top sheet or MTM valuation mini-book.
Staff explain valuation sources or the pricing index where the auditors ask.
The coordinator collects the material and passes it on to the auditors.
Requests are logged in a matrix of all requests for the quarter.

stalls.summary: Requests pass through one coordinator who forwards them to desk staff and waits for the material while the auditors press him, and he concedes some requested information may not come back.
Information discussed the day before was misplaced and had to be asked for again.
Requests reach people who do not cover that desk and are redirected, to Pat Ryder for West desk items and to the real time coordinator for West Hourly deals.
A desk responder says staff were told by risk management never to question the auditors, so requests are worked as asked rather than challenged.

contradictions.summary: The mail names two different people for West desk audit follow-up: the coordinator sends West desk requests to Pat Ryder, while a desk reply says the West Hourly deals in question can be researched by Kate Symes.

automation.approach: A shared request log extending the quarterly matrix, recording each auditor request, the desk owner it is routed to and its status; a routing table by desk naming who answers West desk and real time hourly requests; and standard pulls from the trading and risk systems for the recurring items, such as month-end P&L top sheets, deal tickets with confirmations and MTM mini-books.
automation.rationale: Most rounds ask for the same few document types through one coordinator, and the mail shows requests misrouted, misplaced and pressed for. A written procedure naming who answers for each desk and which standard pull answers each request type cuts the forwarding and re-asking. Valuation explanations still need people.

work_estimate.rationale: Each round means locating and pulling deal tickets or a month-end P&L top sheet, preparing an MTM valuation mini-book, identifying the index used, or writing a short description of where a deal's value comes from, plus keeping the request matrix. A single document pull is about 20 minutes; a multi-deal list or valuation write-up can reach 120; mid 45. Document pulls and logging are repetitive; explanations are not.

processes.description: Pipeline marketing staff negotiate operational balancing agreements (OBAs) with connecting pipelines and producers. A round circulates draft contract language, such as the tolerance-level paragraph, for internal review; works through the counterparty's conditions for signing, such as changing the party name on the contract; and waits for the counterparty to sign and mail back the agreement. Old imbalances under a prior OBA may be cashed out by the other pipeline.
steps: Draft or revise OBA language, such as the tolerance-level paragraph, and circulate it internally for review.
Send the draft agreement to the connecting pipeline or producer.
Resolve the counterparty's conditions for signing, such as changing the name on the contract.
Wait for the counterparty to execute and mail back the agreement.
Settle any old imbalance under the prior agreement, for example by cash-out.

stalls.summary: An OBA stays outstanding until the counterparty's condition is met: the producer will only execute once the name on the contract is changed.
Execution waits on the counterparty mailing the signed agreement back on its own timing.
An imbalance under an old OBA was carried open until the connecting pipeline moved to cash it out.

automation.approach: A standard OBA form with pre-approved clause options for tolerance levels and imbalance cash-out, and a status tracker listing each outstanding agreement, the counterparty condition holding it, when it was sent and any open imbalance, so follow-ups and contract name changes are visible without searching mail.
automation.rationale: The work is contract drafting and counterparty follow-up. A form with pre-approved clauses shortens drafting and internal review, and a tracker addresses the main delays, which are agreements left unsigned on the counterparty's side. Negotiated terms and imbalance settlement still need people.

work_estimate.rationale: Minutes go to drafting or revising clause language such as the tolerance paragraph, amending the contract party name before execution, and checking the old imbalance before a cash-out. A name change is about 20 minutes; drafting negotiated clause language with review can reach 180; mid 60. Only the boilerplate and tracking are repetitive; negotiated terms are not.
